prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and the identity of its active form, which made incretin-based treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity possible

statement.case_for: I opened with the unfolded protein response first and GLP-1 second, and five colleagues put GLP-1 first. Having re-read their arguments I move GLP-1 to the top of my preferred configuration. It is the most complete arc on the shortlist: gut hormone physiology (Holst), proglucagon-derived peptide biology and gut and islet actions (Drucker), and identification and synthesis of the active truncated peptide (Mojsov), followed by outcome trials that show durable benefit in type 2 diabetes and obesity and emerging cardiovascular and renal signals. It is also a discovery in physiology in the most literal sense, and its CNS appetite-circuit side shows how far the biology reaches. My preference is not mainly a function of the size of the opening majority; the scientific and clinical case is independently strong and timely.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. Four credited names cannot fit within three laureates, the Habener group is outside the supplied credit, and Mojsov's role in the active GLP-1(7-36) form carries a priority dispute that I can only partly resolve from recollection. Choosing physiology over drug development also leaves Knudsen out, and a prize built on basic discovery could be seen as slighting the people who made the drugs. The unfolded protein response (B002) has a much cleaner two-person credit (Mori and Walter) and a mechanistic originality that GLP-1 cannot match, and I would regard a UPR prize as fully defensible. Its main weakness is that clinical translation is still early, which matters less for a basic-mechanism prize.

responses.point: Perlmann proposes the physiology trio of Holst, Drucker and Mojsov and says Knudsen's industrial drug development is better recognised through the therapeutic route than through the discovery prize.
responses.response: I agree on the trio but I do not think the Knudsen question is settled so simply. The therapeutic-route argument only holds if the committee is willing to honour the drug-development arm separately, and with a three-person cap and no other shortlisted incretin ballot there is no such route in this configuration. Excluding Knudsen is therefore a real cost, not a neutral choice. I accept it because the prize should reward discovery of the hormone's physiology and active form, and the citation is worded so that it does not claim credit for the drugs themselves.

responses.point: Svenningsson ranks optogenetics third and chooses Deisseroth, Hegemann and Miesenböck as a trio spanning the concept, the molecular tool and neuronal application.
responses.response: I disagree with the trio. As I recall it, Miesenböck's earlier approach used a multi-component system rather than a single light-gated channel. I think the channelrhodopsin discovery (Nagel, Hegemann, with Bamberg) is the core and the neuronal demonstration (Boyden, Deisseroth) the decisive application. Leaving Nagel out in favour of Miesenböck drops the molecular discovery that made the method general. My own trio of Hegemann, Nagel and Deisseroth also omits Bamberg and Boyden, so I concede that no three-person split of B004 is free of a visible injustice. This is why I list it as an alternative rather than prefer it.

responses.point: Sandberg notes that the credit in GLP-1 is the hard part: Mojsov's identification of the active form is decisive but contested, and Habener-group work and Knudsen's chemistry lie outside a clean trio.
responses.response: I share the concern and would add that the contested step is a priority question, not only a fairness one. If the committee cannot document who first identified and characterised the active GLP-1(7-36) form, the safer course is to anchor the citation on Holst's physiology and Drucker's biology and treat Mojsov's place as the open issue. I would still include Mojsov, since peptide identification and synthesis were enabling for the therapeutic programme, but I would want the written evidence checked before any final vote.

responses.point: Linnarsson sees GLP-1 as a coherent arc and treats the exclusion of Knudsen and of the Habener group as a real fairness problem, suggesting basic discovery and drug development might be better recognised separately.
responses.response: I agree that this is a fairness problem. But splitting into two prize parts under the three-person cap would leave a part with a single laureate and make it hard to combine GLP-1 with a second achievement such as B002. I think the committee should accept that a three-person physiology prize cannot reflect everyone and state the limits openly rather than stretching the citation to cover the drug.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov or the Habener group has priority for identification of the active truncated GLP-1 peptide; I rely on recalled facts, not verified evidence.
Whether the committee should recognise drug development (Knudsen) in the same prize or leave it unrecognised.
Whether the mammalian PERK and ATF6 contributions weaken the clean two-person credit I used for B002.
Whether the long-term safety and durability of incretin therapy will change the maturity assessment.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the shortlisted candidates. My motor-circuit research does not tie me to GLP-1, UPR or optogenetics. I note a documented 2009 co-authored paper with Thomas Perlmann and a 2019 synthesis with Sten Grillner, but neither concerns the credited names.
